my-website.summary: A React (TypeScript) single-page application that handles all user interaction. Deployed to Azure Static Web Apps, which serves the static build and rewrites all navigation to index.html so client-side routing works on deep links. Autocomplete on the Trail Finder search bar is powered by the Google Maps JS SDK running entirely in the browser.
my-website.description: A React (TypeScript) single-page application that hosts all user-facing features. Deployed to Azure Static Web Apps with a rewrite rule that sends all navigation to index.html so client-side routing works on deep links.
features: Digits — daily number puzzle game. Uses hardcoded stub data in development (no API call needed)
Momentum Finder — live NBA game cards with momentum shift indicators
Trail Finder — city search with Google Maps autocomplete (browser-side), trail recommendations, weather, and AI-generated gear list
Ideas Board — EasyAuth sign-in, feature idea list and project management, one-click bot trigger

architecture.overview: Create React App with TypeScript and client-side routing via react-router-dom. Each route maps to a top-level TSX + CSS pair. A shared NavBar component appears on every view. REACT_APP_* environment variables are injected at build time by GitHub Actions.

Digits uses process.env.NODE_ENV === "development" to skip the API and use hardcoded stub data locally
Trail Finder autocomplete uses the Google Maps JS SDK entirely in the browser — no backend round-trip, 300ms debounce
Every PR to main gets an isolated SWA preview environment, torn down automatically when the PR closes
Cross-repo deploy: after each backend service deploys, it commits updated metadata to this repo, triggering a frontend rebuild so the Architecture page stays current

ideas-bot.summary: Container App Job triggered by ideas-api. Clones the target repository, runs an AI-driven tool-use loop to implement the requested feature, commits the result, and opens a draft pull request on GitHub. The job scales to zero between invocations.
ideas-bot.description: A containerised Python agent that autonomously implements feature ideas. Triggered on demand by [[ideas-api|ideas-api]], it clones the target repo, runs a GPT-4o tool-use loop to read/write files and execute shell commands, commits the result, and opens a draft pull request. The bot also interacts with ideas-api to manage idea statuses and updates, ensuring smooth coordination across projects. Recent updates enforce stricter project resolution, requiring all ideas to link to a registered project, improving consistency and traceability.
features: App-level retry mechanism for GPT-4o API calls with up to 4 attempts and exponential backoff (60/120/300s) to handle sustained 429 rate limits
Sliding context window for GPT-4o tool-use loop now trims older exchanges beyond the last 14 to reduce token growth and further mitigate 429 risks
Decomposes complex ideas into 2–4 focused sub-tasks, each assigned to the correct project based on repo-specific work, reducing token usage and API load
Sub-tasks are now ordered and can be chained with hard dependencies, ensuring backend tasks complete before dependent frontend tasks
Reduced token caps for tool outputs and agent loops: bash output capped at 2500 chars, read_file capped at 4000 chars, and max_tokens reduced to 4096
Fetches CLAUDE.md from the target repository before the clarity check and agent execution, injecting repo-specific context to improve decision-making and reduce unnecessary questions
Prior Q&A from previous triggers is now fetched and injected into the clarity check, preventing repeated questions and improving efficiency

Added query_table tool for read-only access to Azure Table Storage, enabling the agent to inspect live ideas, projects, and updates tables to validate assumptions and understand record shapes before writing code
Increased agent round limit from 40 to 60, with a wrap-up nudge injected at round 50 to preserve partial work and ensure progress is committed before hitting the limit
Agent now surfaces a summary explanation when no commits are made, allowing users to understand why no changes were implemented and providing actionable feedback
Added support for posting to the Writing API (quixotry.me) via a subprocess helper function, enabling the bot to create posts headlessly using a pre-warmed token cache

architecture.overview: Modular Bicep files deployed at subscription scope. Each service has its own module. The Container App Environment module creates the shared Log Analytics workspace used for unified observability across all Container Apps. The arch-content-foundry module provisions an OpenAI resource with a GPT-4o deployment for the arch-content-update CI workflow. The gpt-5.3-codex model for ideas-bot is deployed independently to avoid quota-related deployment failures impacting the rest of the infrastructure. The history-api module introduces a Go-based Azure Function app running on a Flex Consumption plan, with EasyAuth integration and dedicated storage resources for versions table and history-attachments blob container. The posts-api module now integrates with history-api via HISTORY_API_URL and HISTORY_API_KEY app settings, enabling version history and storage functionality.

  - Requests are routed to the History API using the `HISTORY_API_URL` and authenticated with `HISTORY_API_KEY`.

authentication.title: Authentication
authentication.summary: How user and machine identity is verified across the system: mostly server-side Google ID token validation, with Azure EasyAuth exceptions and machine key support for specific APIs.
authentication.description: Most backend services validate a Google ID token themselves, server-side, on every request — no session state, no cookies, just a Bearer token checked against Google's public keys. Some services, such as ideas-api and history-api, use Azure's EasyAuth for token validation at the platform level, which reduces application code but requires configuration in Azure. Machine authentication via custom headers is supported for specific bot-driven workflows in APIs like ideas-api and history-api, and should be implemented thoughtfully and documented clearly.

sections.heading: Google ID token (application-level)
sections.content: posts-api, learning-plan-api, and dashboard-api all validate the caller's Google ID token themselves, in application code, via the google-auth library — checking the token's signature and audience against one or more configured Google OAuth client IDs. This is the default pattern for any new backend service: no Azure-specific auth wiring, works identically whether the caller is the web app or a CLI tool, and keeps auth logic visible and testable in the service's own codebase rather than delegated to platform configuration.

sections.heading: Azure EasyAuth (platform-level)
sections.content: ideas-api and history-api rely on Azure Functions' built-in EasyAuth: Azure validates the Google ID token at the platform layer before the request ever reaches application code, then injects the validated identity as a request header. This approach reduces the amount of authentication code in the application itself but requires configuration in Azure Function App settings, which can complicate future migrations or debugging. Additionally, both ideas-api and history-api support machine authentication via custom headers (e.g., X-Ideas-Key for ideas-api and HISTORY_WRITE_KEY for history-api) to enable bot-driven workflows alongside user-based authentication.

sections.heading: Machine-to-machine authentication
sections.content: Machine authentication via custom headers is supported for specific bot-driven workflows. For example, history-api supports machine authentication using the HISTORY_WRITE_KEY header, which is now also used by posts-api for machine-to-machine communication. This pattern is useful for scenarios where services need to interact directly without user involvement, such as posts-api's integration with history-api for version history operations. When implementing machine authentication, ensure keys are securely managed and clearly documented.

sections.heading: General philosophy
sections.content: Prefer application-level Google ID token validation for new services — it's portable, testable, and doesn't depend on Azure-specific platform configuration a future migration would need to reproduce. EasyAuth is not being actively adopted further; it's a historical choice on ideas-api and a requirement for history-api due to its Flex Consumption plan and Go runtime. Machine authentication via custom headers can be useful for specific bot-driven workflows but should be implemented thoughtfully and documented clearly.
